passage: Our neighbour's daughter Noor was crying on the steps last week, and it reminded me of something, Imran. When I was young, my brother Anil said, "I'm sorry you feel that way," after he read my diary. I felt worse, because it sounded like it was my fault for being upset. I stopped speaking to him for a week. Years later I made the same mistake with my own son, saying, "Sorry, but you also left the door open." I saw him go still. I said, "Wait. I'm sorry I read your letter. No but. It was wrong of me." His shoulders came down. Listen for the 'but', beta. A real apology has nothing hanging on the end.

qa.q: What did Anil say after he read the narrator's diary?
qa.a: He said, "I'm sorry you feel that way."

qa.q: Why did the narrator feel worse after Anil's apology?
qa.a: It sounded as if being upset was the narrator's own fault, so the narrator felt blamed rather than heard, and was hurt enough to stop speaking to Anil for a week.

qa.q: What did the narrator learn to do differently?
qa.a: The narrator learned to say sorry for the act itself and drop the 'but'.

qa.q: How might Anil have felt about his own words?
qa.a: He may have thought he was apologising, without noticing how it sounded. 🙂

grounding: A conditional apology sounds like blame shifting, and an apology without excuses works better.

passage: The school canteen was deafening, plates clattering and a match blaring from the TV. Hrithik leaned across the table and shouted, "Sorry, but you also ignored my messages!" Tejas heard the word 'but' clearly. He put down his samosa. Was this an apology or a complaint dressed up? His neck felt warm, though he kept his voice level. "I'll answer for my part. But can you say the sorry part without the 'also'?" Hrithik blinked. "Okay. I'm sorry I said your project was boring. That was unkind." He paused. "And I still felt ignored." Tejas nodded. "Thank you. Let's talk about that one properly outside." They took their trays to the corridor, where it was quiet.

qa.q: Where were Tejas and Hrithik when Hrithik shouted his apology?
qa.a: They were in the noisy school canteen.

qa.q: What might Tejas have felt when he heard Hrithik say sorry but you also?
qa.a: He felt his neck get warm, which suggests he felt blamed and irritated, and he wondered whether it was really an apology. He kept his voice steady, so he may also have wanted to fix it.

qa.q: What did Tejas do that helped?
qa.a: He calmly asked Hrithik to say the sorry without the added complaint, then moved the harder conversation somewhere quiet.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see his first attempt?
qa.a: He may have thought he was being fair by naming both sides, without realising it sounded like blame.

grounding: A conditional non-apology is spotted and turned into a plain apology.

passage:
Aparna found out from the lunch queue that Arohi had told the group about her crush on the new boy in 11B. By sixth period, three people had made jokes.
After school, at the bus stop outside the mall, Arohi said, "Look, I'm sorry you feel that way. I didn't think it was such a big secret."
Aparna felt her face go hot. "That's not an apology. That's saying I'm the problem for feeling it."
Arohi opened her mouth, then shut it.
"You told something I asked you not to tell," Aparna said. "That's the bit I need you to say."
The bus came and went. Arohi stood there, fiddling with her bag strap.
"Okay. I told your secret. You asked me not to, and I did it anyway. I'm sorry. No excuse."
Aparna breathed out. "Thank you. That's the one I needed."

qa.q: Where did Aparna and Arohi talk after school?
qa.a: They talked at the bus stop outside the mall.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when Arohi said "I'm sorry you feel that way"?
qa.a: Aparna felt hurt and angry, her face hot, because the words seemed to put the blame on her feelings instead of on what Arohi did.

qa.q: What made Arohi's second apology work?
qa.a: It named exactly what she did, admitted she knew it was wrong, and had no excuse attached.

qa.q: How might Arohi have been feeling as she fiddled with her bag strap?
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed and uncomfortable, realising her first apology had shifted blame and that she needed to own what she did.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager spotting a conditional non-apology and asking for one without excuses.

passage:
"Suraj, about the match. Sorry I shouted, but you also dropped two catches."
Suraj stopped rolling up the mat. "So that's a sorry?"
"Yes! I said sorry."
"You said sorry, but. Everything after 'but' was the real message."
Jagdish frowned. "But you did drop them."
"I know I did. I felt terrible. Then you screamed at me in front of the whole ground. Those are two different things."
Jagdish rubbed his neck. The practice net swayed in the wind.
"Okay. Try again?"
"Go on."
"I shouted at you in front of everyone. That was wrong. Sorry."
"No 'but'?"
"No 'but'."
Suraj nodded. "Thanks. And for the record, I'm staying for extra catching practice."
"I'll throw," Jagdish said.

qa.q: How many catches did Suraj drop?
qa.a: Suraj dropped two catches.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel about the first apology?
qa.a: Suraj felt that it was really blame with a sorry in front, and hurt that the shouting in front of everyone was being excused.

qa.q: What would you advise Jagdish to remember next time he apologises?
qa.a: Leave out the "but" and name only what he did wrong; the other person's mistake can be a separate conversation.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have seen his first apology?
qa.a: Jagdish probably thought it was fair and complete, because he was still annoyed about the catches and didn't notice the "but" was shifting blame.

grounding: The dialogue shows a "sorry, but you also" non-apology being spotted and replaced with one without excuses.

passage:
Last Diwali, my younger cousin Urmila spent a whole evening building a rangoli outside Nani's door, and I stepped right through the middle of it with muddy chappals, laughing at my phone.
She burst into tears. I said, "Sorry if you're upset, but you shouldn't have made it right in front of the door."
I thought that was an apology. Nani didn't. She pulled me into the kitchen and said, "Tenzin, you said sorry to her feelings and then blamed her. Where was the sorry for your feet?"
I was annoyed, but I kept hearing it.
So I went back out. Urmila was sweeping up the colours. I said, "I walked through your rangoli without looking. That was careless. I'm sorry." Then I knelt down and helped her redo the border.
She didn't say much. But she handed me the yellow powder.

qa.q: What did the narrator step through with muddy chappals?
qa.a: Tenzin stepped right through the middle of Urmila's rangoli with muddy chappals.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when she handed Tenzin the yellow powder?
qa.a: She seemed to be softening, still a little hurt but ready to forgive, letting Tenzin help rebuild the rangoli.

qa.q: Which turning point changed Tenzin's apology?
qa.a: Nani pointing out that the first apology blamed Urmila; Tenzin then went back and apologised plainly for being careless.

qa.q: How might Nani have seen the first apology?
qa.a: Nani saw it as blame shifting, sorry for Urmila's feelings but not for the act, which is why she stepped in.

grounding: The account shows a conditional non-apology being named and replaced by a plain apology without excuses.

passage:
Coach's notebook, under-16 girls, Saturday
Friction at practice again. Aadhya passed to Gurpreet late in the scrimmage, the ball went out, and Aadhya shouted, "Are you even awake?" Gurpreet walked off the court. When I brought them together, Aadhya folded her arms and said, "I'm sorry you feel that way. But you also didn't call for it." Gurpreet's jaw tightened; she looked at the floor and said, "Fine." It was not fine. I asked Aadhya to listen to her own words again and tell me who that sorry was really for. She went quiet, then said, "It's kind of blaming her." I suggested she try it with no "but". Second try: "I shouted at you in front of everyone. That was wrong. I'm sorry." Gurpreet gave a small nod. They ran the next drill together without a word. I'll watch how the week goes before Sunday's match.

qa.q: What did Aadhya shout during the scrimmage?
qa.a: Aadhya shouted, "Are you even awake?"

qa.q: What did Gurpreet's tight jaw and 'Fine' suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Gurpreet likely still felt hurt and blamed, since the apology turned the fault back on her. It might also have been embarrassment after being shouted at in front of everyone.

qa.q: What made Aadhya's second apology stronger?
qa.a: It named exactly what she did, called it wrong and dropped the 'but', so it apologised without excuses.

qa.q: How might Aadhya have seen her first apology?
qa.a: Aadhya may have thought 'I'm sorry you feel that way' counted as sorry, until the coach's question showed it was really blaming Gurpreet.

grounding: It shows a teenager giving a conditional 'sorry you feel that way, but' apology and learning to give one without excuses.
